introduction: On this Sunday, Isaiah tells the fearful, Be strong, do not fear, your God will come to save you; then the ears of the deaf will be opened. In the Gospel, Jesus takes a deaf man aside, touches his ears and tongue, and says, Ephphatha, be opened. Saint James warns us not to favor the rich over the poor. Let us ask the Lord to open our ears to his word and our hearts to every person.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord opens the eyes of the blind and raises up those who are bowed down. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may welcome rich and poor alike, without favoritism. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the deaf, the blind and all who live with disabilities: that they may be fully included in our communities. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are afraid: that they may hear God's word, Be strong, do not fear. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those whose ears are closed to God's word: that the Lord may open them, as he opened the ears of the deaf man. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that our ears may be open to hear God's word and our tongues free to proclaim it. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your Son opened the ears of the deaf and loosened the tongue of the mute. Open our hearts to your word, and help us to treat every person with equal love. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Ephphatha
reflection.body:
Isaiah speaks to a frightened people: "Be strong! Don't be afraid! Behold, your God will come." When God comes, everything that is broken will be healed: "Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped." Even the desert will burst into life.

In the Gospel, people bring Jesus a man who is deaf and has a speech impediment. Jesus does not heal him in front of the crowd. He takes him aside, privately, and communicates with him in a way he can understand: he puts his fingers into his ears and touches his tongue. Then "Looking up to heaven, he sighed," and said, "Ephphatha!" which means "Be opened!" At once the man can hear and speak clearly.

The crowd's reaction echoes the first reading: "He has done all things well. He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" What Isaiah promised is happening.

The word Ephphatha is still used in the rite of Baptism. The priest may touch the ears and mouth of the newly baptized, praying that they may soon hear God's word and proclaim their faith. Each of us needs that opening again and again.

Saint James shows one way our hearts can be closed. If a rich man and a poor man come into church, and we give the rich man a good seat and tell the poor man to stand, "haven't you shown partiality among yourselves?" And he reminds us: "Didn't God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith?"

This week, ask Jesus to say Ephphatha to you: to open your ears to his word and to the people you tend not to hear. And notice who is overlooked in your parish or workplace, and make them welcome.
